field_sets.expect: This entry presents the Laurentian narrative and Creighton's later nationalism. Read on 2026-10-14: his 1957 presidential address (pp. 1–12) and his 1969 lecture 'The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence' (pp. 14–25), both in full from page images; Dominion of the North (1944) at its contents and selected pages (pp. 21, 24–25, 166, 270, 272, 298, 419, 505–507) in an open Internet Archive copy. The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) itself is unread: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only, and its argument is checked through the 1944 book, his own 1969 retrospect (labelled as such) and the first page of Herbert Heaton's 1938 review. He is not presented as the founder of a school: in 1969 he reported that others regarded the 1937 phrase as 'the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school' and the 'genesis' of 'the Laurentian interpretation', and said only that he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea'. The Innis lineage is recorded as contested: readers from Woodcock (1979) and Ouellet (1984) to Salmon (1997) tie the book to Innis's staple studies, while Creighton said the subject was suggested by W. P. M. Kennedy, 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time'. The 1957 and 1969 texts are polemics; their judgements of Mackenzie King, Quebec and bilingualism are recorded as his claims, not adopted. Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) and his later hinterland critique are known here only through Davis (1985); Careless's 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism' (1954), Berger's chapter on Creighton (1976), Canada's First Century (1970) and the Innis biography (1957) are unread (catalogue or review level only).
